description: We are a team "Git Push to Space" in Cottbus with skills in AI, software and mobile development, data pipelines and architecture. We are building a fire calendar that joins 25 years of NASA satellite fire records from two different sensors into one consistent history, so anyone can see whether fire activity in a region is normal or unusual. The data pipeline already runs on real NASA data. We have room for one more teammate, ideally in Earth science, statistics or design.
summary:
FireChronos turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent record that anyone can explore as a calendar.

NASA has detected fires from space with MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. VIIRS's sharper view records about three times more detections for the same fires, so the raw record jumps in 2012 and falsely suggests rising fire activity. We harmonized the two sensors on a 0.25° grid using 624 NASA FIRMS files for 16 European countries, 2001–2025. We measured the VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio while both flew (2012–2021) and tested it on unseen years (2022–2025). The Europe-wide gap fell from 70% to under 5%, and R² rose from 0.50 to 0.94.
Our web app shows fire activity by year and month for any country or drawn area, with maps, trends, findings and an accuracy table.
This matters because uncorrected data misleads: in 8 of 16 countries, a significant "rise" in fire disappears after harmonization. FireChronos helps fire services, researchers and planners see real seasons, anomalies and trends.
details:
FireChronos turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire observations into one comparable record, shown as an interactive fire calendar for Europe.

NASA's MODIS sensors (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) detect fires by their heat. VIIRS has finer pixels (375 m against 1 km) and records about three times more detections for the same fires. Raw data therefore jumps in 2012, creating false trends.

Our pipeline downloads 624 NASA FIRMS files for 16 European countries (2001–2025). It keeps presumed vegetation fires with adequate confidence and counts detections on a 0.25° grid per month. From 2012–2021, when both sensors flew, we measured how much more VIIRS detects: a factor of 3.163. MODIS years are scaled by it, so all 25 years share the VIIRS scale. From 2012 on, the record uses actual VIIRS measurements.

We validated on unseen years (2022–2025). Raw MODIS was 70% below VIIRS across Europe; the corrected record was within 5%, and R² rose from 0.50 to 0.94.

The web app lets users:

  • view a year × month fire calendar for Europe, any country, a searched place, or an area drawn on the map, including across borders;
  • click a month to see where detections occurred, on a 2D map or a rotatable globe;
  • switch between raw and corrected records to see the 2012 artifact disappear;
  • read plain-language findings: main fire season, worst year, and how a month compares with its historical median;
  • see trend tests, extent charts and which areas burn repeatedly;
  • see the correction's accuracy per country, with warnings where it is weaker.

Benefits and intended impact

Without harmonization, trend analysis is misleading. In 8 of 16 countries, raw data shows a significant rise in fire activity that disappears after correction, and in two countries a rise turns into a fall. FireChronos helps:

  • fire services and forest managers judge whether a month is unusual and when their fire season peaks;
  • researchers and journalists check real trends instead of sensor artifacts;
  • planners identify places that burn year after year.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP active fire data).
  • Processing: Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (validation metrics), Matplotlib.
  • Web app: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS.
  • Maps and charts: MapLibre GL with OpenFreeMap tiles, terra-draw for drawing areas, Apache ECharts.
  • Places: GeoNames for nearest-town names, Open-Meteo geocoding for place search.
  • Quality: Vitest unit tests that recompute published results from the data.
  • Hosting: Vercel. No database and no API keys; it runs in any browser, on desktop and mobile.

Creativity

  • A calendar view: it makes 25 years of seasons, anomalies and trends visible at a glance.
  • A raw/corrected switch: it turns an abstract data problem into something anyone can see.
  • Regions that cross borders: analysis follows the landscape, not national boundaries.
  • Accuracy shown inside the app: users see where the method is reliable and where it is not.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity: testing on held-out years, clearly marking estimated years before 2012, and stating limits. The correction cannot add fires MODIS missed; detections are not individual fires; accuracy is lower in central and northern Europe.
  • Usability: plain language, fast loading (one file per country), accessible controls and mobile support.
  • Data and privacy: proper attribution and open licences; location is requested only when the user asks.
